title: Iran Weighs Nuclear Options as U.S. Pressure Mounts and Talks Stall
excerpt: Tehran's leadership openly debates pursuing a nuclear weapon or seeking sanctions relief as Washington's naval blockade and strikes tighten, and Israel warns an Iranian move could spiral out of control.
body:
• Iran's leadership is openly debating whether to pursue a nuclear weapon, leave the Non-Proliferation Treaty, or curtail its program in exchange for sanctions relief, as a protracted conflict with the United States continues.
  • Washington is choking Iran's economy through a naval blockade and sanctions, and recently struck Iranian oil tankers linked to the Revolutionary Guard; Tehran retaliated with missile strikes on U.S. bases in Jordan.
  • Iran has barred inspections of its core nuclear sites since U.S. and Israeli strikes in June 2025, which Tehran's critics say did not destroy its large stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
  • A senior Israeli defense official said Iran's room for maneuver has narrowed, while Israel prepares for the possibility that an Iranian move could spiral out of control.

Iran is weighing its next move against the United States and Israel as nuclear negotiations stall and American pressure on its economy deepens. A senior Israeli defense official said Tehran's room for maneuver has narrowed under Washington's sanctions and naval blockade, while Israel is preparing for the possibility that an Iranian move could spiral out of control, according to the Jerusalem Post.

Inside Iran, meanwhile, a once-taboo debate about whether to build a nuclear weapon has burst into the open. Lawmakers introduced a fast-track bill in parliament calling for Iran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, a step only taken by North Korea before it built nuclear weapons, the Wall Street Journal reported. Top officials have begun discussing weaponization in terms not of whether it should happen, but whether it can be achieved before being detected.

Context & Background

The current confrontation began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities in June 2025. President Trump said the attacks obliterated Iran's nuclear program, though Tehran retained a large stockpile of highly enriched uranium and underground sites where work could be revived, according to the Wall Street Journal. An interim deal fell apart in June, and sporadic direct fighting between Iran and the U.S. has continued since.

Iran has refused inspections of its core nuclear sites since the bombings. Before the strikes, experts believed Iran could build a nuclear weapon within months; it had produced enough 60%-enriched uranium to fuel around 11 weapons. The regime's formal stance was governed by a fatwa that Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, killed in February, issued two decades ago banning weapons of mass destruction — but that restraint is now openly questioned.

Iranian officials had earlier been close to compromise. One high-level Middle East official told the Wall Street Journal that Iran nearly agreed to concessions on its nuclear program during negotiations involving JD Vance. Tehran offered a 10-year enrichment freeze in exchange for sanctions lifting, but the talks collapsed and military exchanges escalated instead.

Last week, U.S. forces struck several Iranian oil tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Iran retaliated by firing a barrage of missiles toward American military bases in Jordan, a further step in a cycle of strikes that has now lasted well over a year.

Impact & Analysis

The debate in Tehran reflects a collapse of the regime's old nuclear threshold policy — maintaining the capability to build a bomb without assembling one. Critics in Iran say that approach proved the worst of both worlds: it failed to deter Washington and Jerusalem and instead gave them a pretext to bomb Iran's facilities, according to the Wall Street Journal.

"The debate about the bomb is largely now whether we can do it rather than whether we should do it."

— Hamidreza Azizi, Senior Analyst, International Crisis Group

Yet the obstacles to weaponization have sharpened alongside the desire. The destruction of enrichment sites, the killing of nuclear scientists, and the bombing of yellowcake and centrifuge factories over the past 16 months were major setbacks. U.S. and Israeli intelligence have demonstrated deep penetration of Iran's nuclear work, meaning any breakout attempt would likely be detected before completion. As Raz Zimmt of Israel's Institute for National Security Studies told the Journal, Iran currently lacks missile-deliverable warheads and the command structures needed for rapid nuclear decision-making.

Some Iranian officials argue that the country's grip over the Strait of Hormuz — through which much of the world's oil flows — is a less risky and sufficient deterrent than a bomb. That leverage, however, is exactly what Washington is trying to neutralize with its naval blockade.

Diaspora Angle

For India, which imports the vast majority of its crude oil through sea routes touching the Gulf, a sustained conflict in the Strait of Hormuz translates directly into higher fuel prices and inflation at home. Millions of Indians work in the Gulf states that sit within range of Iran's missiles, making any escalation a concern for families across the diaspora.

What's Next

President Masoud Pezeshkian told India Today that Tehran is ready to return to negotiations if Washington lifts sanctions and abandons what he called the language of force. "We don't know which of the things Trump says we are ultimately supposed to accept and stand by," he said. Trump, writing on Truth Social, insisted Iran urgently wants a deal and that he alone would decide whether the U.S. engages.

U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz said Washington rejected Iran's proposed seven-day ceasefire because Tehran sought access to frozen assets and an end to the blockade. The Israeli defense official's warning — that Iran's narrowing options raise the risk of a move that spirals — keeps a diplomatic off-ramp open while preparing for the opposite outcome. The next few weeks of indirect contact will determine whether the stalemate breaks toward negotiation or toward another round of strikes.
